'''Paul Ralph Ehrlich''' (May 29, 1932 – March 13, 2026) was an American biologist, author, and environmentalist<ref>{{cite web |url=https://nicholas.duke.edu/news/biologist-paul-ehrlich-author-population-bomb-speak-oct-18 |title=Biologist Paul Ehrlich, Author of The Population Bomb to Speak on Oct. 18 |work=Duke University}}</ref> known for his predictions and warnings about the consequences of [[population growth]], including [[famine]] and [[resource depletion]].<ref name="Haberman"/><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/why-didnt-first-earth-days-predictions-come-true-its-complicated-180958820/ | title=Why Didn't the First Earth Day's Predictions Come True? It's Complicated|work=Smithsonian Magazine|first=Hannah|last=Waters|date=April 22, 2016|access-date=March 13, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Mieszkowski |first=Katharine |url=https://www.salon.com/2008/09/17/population_control/ |title=Do we need population control? |work=[[Salon (website)|Salon]] |date=September 17, 2008 |archive-date=October 27, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111027001145/http://www.salon.com/2008/09/17/population_control/ |url-status=live |access-date=September 27, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |title=The Population Bust: Demographic Decline and the End of Capitalism as We Know It |magazine=Foreign Affairs |date=September 2019 |quote=Ehrlich's prophecy, of course, proved wrong, for reasons that [[Darrell Bricker|Bricker]] and [[John Ibbitson|Ibbitson]] elegantly chart in Empty Planet.}}</ref> Ehrlich was the Bing Professor of [[Population study|Population Studies]] of the Department of Biology of [[Stanford University]]. He started working at [[Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve]] in 1959. He along with many other biology professors, led the efforts for Stanford University to designate and protect Jasper Ridge in 1973 as a biological preserve and as a long-term research facility for faculty and students.<ref name="leaders"/><ref name="tierney1990" />

Ehrlich became well known for the controversial 1968 book ''[[The Population Bomb]],'' which he co-authored with his wife [[Anne H. Ehrlich]], in which they famously stated that "[i]n the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death in spite of any crash programs embarked upon now."<ref name="leaders">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oHYD-XUiSBEC&pg=PA318| title=Leaders from the 1960s: A Biographical Sourcebook of American Activism |publisher=Greenwood Press, 1994 |page=318 |isbn=978-0-313-27414-5 |year=1994}}</ref><ref name="tierney1990" /> This position has led historians and critics to describe Ehrlich as a [[neo-Malthusian]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Robertson|first=Thomas|date=2012|title=The Malthusian Moment: Global Population Growth and the Birth of American Environmentalism|publisher=Rutgers University Press|pages=126–151|isbn=978-0-8135-5271-2|oclc=746489134}}</ref>

There are mixed views on Ehrlich's assertions on the dangers of expanding human populations.<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--not stated-->|date=June 8, 2015 |title=Is Overpopulation a Legitimate Threat to Humanity and the Planet?|url=https://www.nytimes.com/roomfordebate/2015/06/08/is-overpopulation-a-legitimate-threat-to-humanity-and-the-planet|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=July 30, 2023}}</ref> While statistician Paul A. Murtaugh says that Ehrlich was largely correct,<ref>{{cite news |last=Murtaugh|first=Paul A. |date=June 8, 2015 |title=Paul Ehrlich's Population Bomb Argument Was Right|url=https://www.nytimes.com/roomfordebate/2015/06/08/is-overpopulation-a-legitimate-threat-to-humanity-and-the-planet/paul-ehrlichs-population-bomb-argument-was-right|work=The New York Times |access-date=July 30, 2023|quote=Ehrlich's argument that expanding human populations cannot be sustained on an Earth with finite carrying capacity is irrefutable and, indeed, almost tautological. The only uncertainty concerns the timing and severity of the rebalancing that must inevitably occur.}}</ref> Ehrlich has been criticized for his approach and views, both for their pessimistic outlook and for the failure of his predictions. In 2004, Ehrlich had acknowledged that population growth was in decline, but had believed that [[overconsumption]] by wealthy nations was a major problem. He maintained that his warnings about disease and [[global warming|climate change]] were essentially correct.<ref name="grist" /> Journalist [[Dan Gardner (author)|Dan Gardner]] criticized Ehrlich for his [[cognitive dissonance]] in forecasting, asserting that Ehrlich took credit for his successful predictions but failed to acknowledge his mistakes.<ref name="dg">{{cite book|title=Future Babble: Why Expert Predictions Fail – and Why We Believe Them Anyway|last=Gardner|first=Dan|publisher=McClelland and Stewart|year=2010|location=Toronto|pages=228–236|oclc=694600738|isbn=978-0-7535-2236-3}}</ref>

==Early life, education and academic career==
[[File:Paul R Ehrlich.png|thumb|Ehrlich in 2010]]
Ehrlich was born in [[Philadelphia]], [[Pennsylvania]], the son of William Ehrlich and Ruth Rosenberg. His father was a shirt salesman and his mother was a [[Greek language|Greek]] and [[Latin]] scholar<ref>{{Cite web | title=PAUL EHRLICH | url=http://www.abc.net.au/rn/latenightlive/stories/2009/2747139.htm | work=Radio National | publisher=ABC | access-date=March 4, 2013 | last=Adams | first=Phillip | last2=MacDonald | first2=Kate | date=November 19, 2009}}</ref> and public school teacher.<ref name="leaders" /> Ehrlich's mother's German ancestors arrived in the United States in the 1840s, and his paternal grandparents emigrated there later from the Galician and Transylvanian part of the Austrian Empire.<ref name="Stoll">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bjooDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA260 |title=Inherit the Holy Mountain: Religion and the Rise of American Environmentalism |publisher=Oxford University Press |page=260 |isbn=978-0-19-069794-5 |date=September 15, 2017}}</ref> Ehrlich has been described as having grown up in a household that was Jewish but anti-Zionist.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tal |first=Alon |title=The Blogs: A Life in Defense of the Earth: The Legacy of Paul Ehrlich |url=https://blogs.timesofisrael.com/a-life-in-defense-of-the-earth-the-legacy-of-paul-ehrlich/ |access-date=March 22, 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref> During his childhood his family moved to [[Maplewood, New Jersey]], where he attended [[Columbia High School (New Jersey)|Columbia High School]], graduating in 1949.<ref name="leaders" /><ref>Polner, Murray. [https://books.google.com/books?id=gIl2AAAAMAAJ&dq=%22paul+r.+ehrlich%22+%22columbia+high+school%22 ''American Jewish Biographies''], p. 88. Facts on File, 1982. {{ISBN|9780871964625}}. Accessed August 3, 2019. "his childhood his family moved to Maplewood, New Jersey, where he was graduated from Columbia High School in 1949."</ref>

By training, Ehrlich was an [[entomologist]] specializing in [[Lepidoptera]] (butterflies). He earned a bachelor's degree in [[zoology]] from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] in 1953, an M.A. from the [[University of Kansas]] in 1955, and a Ph.D. from the University of Kansas in 1957, supervised by the prominent [[bee]] researcher [[Charles Duncan Michener]] (the title of his dissertation: ''The Morphology, Phylogeny and Higher Classification of the Butterflies (Lepidoptera: Papilionoidea)'').<ref>Ehrlich, Paul R., "[http://hdl.handle.net/1808/7853 The Morphology, Phylogeny and Higher Classification of the Butterflies (Lepidoptera: Papilionoidea)]," Ph.D. dissertation, University of Kansas, May 1957.</ref>

During his studies he participated in surveys of [[insect]]s in the areas of the [[Bering Sea]] and [[Canadian arctic]], and then, with a [[National Institutes of Health]] fellowship, investigated the genetics and behavior of parasitic [[mite]]s. In 1959 he joined the faculty at [[Stanford University]]. He became well known for popularizing the term [[coevolution]] in an influential 1964 paper co-authored with the botanist [[Peter H. Raven]], where they proposed that reciprocal selective responses between insects and their food plants explains the extreme diversification of plants and insects.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Ehrlich | first1=Paul R. | last2=Raven | first2=Peter H. | year=1964 | title=Butterflies and Plants: A Study in Coevolution | journal=Evolution | volume=18 | issue=4 | pages=586–608 | doi=10.2307/2406212| jstor=2406212}}</ref>

This paper was highly influential on the then-nascent field of [[chemical ecology]]. He was promoted to professor of [[biology]] in 1966, and appointed to the Bing Professorship in 1977.<ref name="cv">{{Cite web | title=PAUL R. EHRLICH | url=http://www.stanford.edu/group/CCB/Staff/Paul%20EhrlichCV.PDF | work=Paul R. Ehrlich Resume | publisher=Stanford University | access-date=March 4, 2013 | last=Ehrlich | first=Paul R. | year=2001}}</ref><ref>Lewis, J. "Biologist Paul R. Ehrlich. Six billion and counting". ''Scientific American'' October 2000, pages 30, 32.</ref> In 1984, he founded the Center for Conservation Biology at Stanford University.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Welcome to the Center for Conservation Biology |url=https://ccb.stanford.edu/ |publisher=Stanford University |access-date=April 4, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230325013426/https://ccb.stanford.edu/ |archive-date=March 25, 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref> He was a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], the United States [[National Academy of Sciences]], the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] and the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref name="cv" />

==Overpopulation debate==
{{Further|Human overpopulation}}
[[File:Population curve.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|A graph showing changes in global human population since 10,000 BC]]
[[File:WorldPopGrowth.png|thumb|upright=1.2|The evidence against a population bomb: Since the 1960s, the world population growth rate has decreased, and is projected to decline further.]]

A lecture that Ehrlich gave on the topic of overpopulation at the [[Commonwealth Club of California]] was broadcast by radio in April 1967.<ref name="turner">{{Cite web |title=Story: Paul Ehrlich, the Vindication of a Public Scholar |url=http://spot.us/pitches/135-paul-ehrlich-the-vindication-of-a-public-scholar/story |work=Spot.us |id=(First published by ''The Earth Island Journal'') |publisher=American Public Media |access-date=March 4, 2013 |last=Turner |first=Tom |year=2011 |archive-date=January 23, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130123173818/http://spot.us/pitches/135-paul-ehrlich-the-vindication-of-a-public-scholar/story }}</ref> The success of the lecture caused further publicity, and the suggestion from [[David Brower]] the executive director of the environmentalist [[Sierra Club]], and [[Ian Ballantine]] of [[Ballantine Books]] to write a book concerning the topic. Ehrlich and his wife, Anne H. Ehrlich, collaborated on the book, ''[[The Population Bomb]]'', but the publisher insisted that a single author be credited; only Paul's name appears as an author.<ref name="The Population Bomb Revisited">{{Cite journal |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Paul R. |last2=Ehrlich |first2=Anne H. |title=The Population Bomb Revisited |url=http://www.populationmedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2009/07/Population-Bomb-Revisited-Paul-Ehrlich-20096.pdf |journal=Electronic Journal of Sustainable Development |year=2009 |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=63–71 |access-date=January 22, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140630024241/http://www.populationmedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2009/07/Population-Bomb-Revisited-Paul-Ehrlich-20096.pdf |archive-date=June 30, 2014 }}</ref>

Although Ehrlich was not the first to warn about population issues&nbsp;— concern had been widespread during the 1950s and 1960s&nbsp;— his charismatic and media-savvy methods helped publicize the topic.<ref name="dg"/> ''[[The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson]]'' had Ehrlich on as a guest more than twenty times, with one interview lasting an hour.<ref>{{cite book |last=Weisman |first=A. |title=Countdown: Our Last, Best Hope for a Future on Earth? |publisher=Little, Brown |year=2013 |isbn=978-0-316-23650-8 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t28FlWXoig0C&pg=PT44 |access-date=January 3, 2023 |page=44}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Pilzer |first=P.Z. |title=God Wants You to Be Rich: How and Why Everyone Can Enjoy Material and Spiritual Wealth in Our Abundant World |publisher=Touchstone |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-4165-4927-7 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-VF7MwIsu6MC&pg=PA49 |access-date=January 3, 2023 |page=49}}</ref>

===Writings===
====''The Population Bomb'' (1968)====
{{Main|The Population Bomb}}

The original edition of ''The Population Bomb'' began with the statement: {{blockquote|''The battle to feed all of humanity is over. In the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death in spite of any crash programs embarked upon now. At this late date nothing can prevent a substantial increase in the world death rate{{nbsp}}...''<ref name="Population Bomb">{{cite book|author=Ehrlich, Paul R.|title=The Population Bomb |url=https://archive.org/details/populationbomb00ehrl |url-access=registration |publisher=Ballantine Books |year=1968}}</ref>}} Ehrlich argued that the human population was too great, and that while the extent of disaster could be mitigated, humanity could not prevent severe [[famine]]s, the [[Epidemic|spread of disease]], [[Civil disorder|social unrest]], and other negative consequences of overpopulation.

Ehrlich has proposed different solutions to the problem of overpopulation. In ''The Population Bomb'' he wrote, "We must have [[population control]] at home, hopefully through a system of incentives and penalties, but by compulsion if voluntary methods fail. We must use our political power to push other countries into programs which combine agricultural development and population control."<ref name="Population Bomb"/> Voluntary measures he has endorsed include the easiest possible availability of [[birth control]] and [[abortion]].

Decades later, Ehrlich's continued prominence and the failure of the book's predictions to materialize led to renewed scrutiny and criticism. ''The New York Times'' said his "apocalyptic predictions fell as flat as ancient theories about the shape of the Earth".<ref name="Haberman" />

Science author [[Charles C. Mann (writer)|Charles C. Mann]] wrote that the book's predictions "fueled an anti-population-growth crusade that led to human rights abuses around the world", including coercive population control policies and even forced sterilizations.<ref name="MannSmithsonian" /> Ehrlich's pointed criticism of India in particular (for instance, emphasizing the overpopulation of [[Delhi]] rather than [[Paris]], which had nearly triple Delhi's population at the time of writing) has been criticized for focusing much more on "feelings" than on actual data.<ref name="MannSmithsonian">{{cite web | url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/book-incited-worldwide-fear-overpopulation-180967499/ | title=The Book That Incited a Worldwide Fear of Overpopulation|work=Smithsonian Magazine|first=Charles C.|last=Mann|date=January 2018|access-date=March 15, 2023}}</ref>

Neither of the Ehrlichs have ever publicly renounced predictions, instead insisting that they were largely correct, despite the errors noted by many experts.{{Dubious|date=May 2023}}<ref name="dg"/>

====''The Population Explosion'' (1990)====
''The Population Explosion'' argues that the population catastrophe outlined in the Ehrlichs' earlier work ''The Population Bomb'' had in fact come to pass, and that "hunger is rife and famine and plague ever more imminent".<ref name="Simcox">{{cite journal |last1=Simcox |first1=David E. |title=Review: The Population Explosion. by Paul Ehrlich and Anne Ehrlich |journal=Population and Environment |date=Dec 1990 |volume=12 |issue=2 |page=159 |doi=10.1007/BF01261480 |jstor=27503187 }}</ref>

Many accepted the premise of a looming population problem; for instance the sociologist [[Frank D. Bean|Frank Bean]] wrote in a review of the book for the ''New York Times'' that "it is not merely prudent but imperative that we confront population issues, and do so now".<ref name="BeanNYT">{{cite news |last1=Bean |first1=Frank D. |title=TOO MANY, TOO RICH, TOO WASTEFUL |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/04/01/books/too-many-too-rich-too-wasteful.html |access-date=March 27, 2024 |date=April 1, 1990}}</ref> Others, like the sociologist [[Thomas J. Espenshade]], criticized the Ehrlichs for an "alarmist" tone.<ref name="Espenshade">{{cite journal |last1=Espenshade |first1=Thomas J. |title=Review: The Population Explosion. by Paul R. Ehrlich and Anne H. Ehrlich |journal=Population and Development Review |date=June 1991 |volume=17 |issue=2 |page=333 |jstor=1973735 }}</ref> The book was also criticised for its approach to family planning, which argued voluntary family planning was insufficient to deal with population growth and government-directed population control was necessary.<ref name="Jacobson">{{cite journal |last1=Jacobson |first1=Jodi L. |title=People vs. the Environment |journal=Family Planning Perspectives |date=Mar–Apr 1991 |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=95–96 |doi=10.2307/2135462 |jstor=2135462 }}</ref> The Ehrlichs were accused of advocating the curtailment of reproductive freedoms and giving the state a larger role in such decisions, while leaving ambiguous "just how authoritarian a solution they are willing to endorse."<ref name="Espenshade" />

Subsequent attention to the book scrutinized its descriptions of an unfolding overpopulation catastrophe. The book's contention that global food production had already peaked proved to be incorrect.<ref name="Lam">{{cite journal |last1=Lam |first1=David |editor1-last=Asefa |editor1-first=Sisay |title=How the World Survived the Population Bomb: An Economic Perspective |journal=The Economics of Sustainable Development |date=2005 |pages=99–132 |url=https://research.upjohn.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?filename=4&article=1170&context=up_press&type=additional |access-date=March 27, 2024 |publisher=Upjohn Institute Press |location=Kalamazoo, MI|doi=10.17848/9781417596324.Ch5 |isbn=978-1-4175-9632-4 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Similarly, the prediction that India faced catastrophic food shortage in the 1990s failed to materialize.<ref name="Lam" />

====''Optimum Human Population Size'' (1994)====
In this paper, the Ehrlichs discussed their opinion on the 'optimal size' for human population, given their assessment of the current technological situation. Their [[back-of-the-envelope calculation|"back-of-the-envelope" estimate]] was that the optimal human population, given "prevailing biophysical and social conditions" and satisfying certain criteria, is "in the vicinity of 1.5 to 2 billion people". They referred to establishing "social policies to influence fertility rates."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Daily |first1=Gretchen C. |last2=Ehrlich |first2=Anne H. |last3=Ehrlich |first3=Paul R. |url=http://dieoff.org/page99.htm |title=Optimum Human Population Size |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170817085428/http://www.dieoff.org/page99.htm |archive-date=August 17, 2017 |journal=Population and Environment: A Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies |volume=15 |number=6 |date=July 1994 |pages=469–475 |publisher=Human Sciences Press|doi=10.1007/BF02211719 |bibcode=1994PopEn..15..469D |s2cid=153761569 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
[[File:Paul R. Ehrlich 2008 (cropped).jpg|thumb|Ehrlich speaking in 2008]]

===After 2000===
During a 2004 interview, Ehrlich answered questions about the predictions he made in ''The Population Bomb''. He acknowledged that some of what he had published had not occurred, but stated that he felt "little embarrassment" and reaffirmed his basic opinion that overpopulation is a major problem. He noted that, "Fifty-eight academies of science said that same thing in 1994, as did the world scientists' warning to humanity in the same year. My view has become depressingly mainline!"<ref name="grist">{{Cite magazine |title=When Paul's Said and Done |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041115081108/http://www.grist.org/comments/interactivist/2004/08/09/ehrlich/index1.html |magazine=Grist Magazine |access-date=September 24, 2015 |last=Ehrlich| first=Paul |url=http://www.grist.org/comments/interactivist/2004/08/09/ehrlich/index1.html |archive-date=November 15, 2004 |date=August 13, 2004 |quote=Some things I predicted have not come to pass.}}</ref> Ehrlich asserted that 600 million people were very hungry while billions were under-nourished, and insisted that his predictions about disease and climate change were essentially correct.<ref name="grist" /> Retrospectively, Ehrlich said that ''The Population Bomb'', which predicted a widespread famine by 1985 that never materialized, was actually "way too optimistic".<ref name="turner" /><ref name="The Population Bomb Revisited" />

In a 2008 discussion hosted by the website [[Salon (website)|''Salon'']], Paul Ehrlich was more critical of the United States specifically, claiming that it should control its population and consumption as an example to the rest of the world. He still professed a belief that governments should discourage people from having more than two children, suggesting, for example, a higher tax rate for larger families.<ref>{{Cite web |work=Salon |url=http://www.salon.com/2008/09/17/population_control/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111027001145/http://www.salon.com/2008/09/17/population_control/ |url-status=live |archive-date=October 27, 2011 |title=Do we need population control? |last=Mieszkowski |first=Katharine |date=September 17, 2008}}</ref>

In 2011, as the world's population passed the seven billion mark, Ehrlich argued that the next two billion people on Earth would cause more damage than the previous two billion, as humans now increasingly would have to resort to using more marginal and environmentally damaging resources.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hall |first=Eleanor |title=Population analyst warns of catastrophe |url=http://www.abc.net.au/worldtoday/content/2011/s3351962.htm |access-date=October 31, 2011 |newspaper=The World Today |date=October 31, 2011}}</ref> As of 2013, Ehrlich continued to perform policy research concerning population and resource issues, with an emphasis upon [[endangered species]], [[cultural evolution]], [[environmental ethics]], and the preservation of [[genetics|genetic]] resources. Along with Dr. Gretchen Daily, he performed work in countryside [[biogeography]]; that is, the study of making human-disturbed areas hospitable to [[biodiversity]]. His research group at Stanford University examined extensive natural populations of the [[Bay checkerspot butterfly]] ({{lang|la|Euphydryas editha bayensis}}).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://jrbp.stanford.edu/db/projects/project_display.php?project_id=80 |title=Longterm studies of the Bay checkerspot butterfly and feasibility of reintroduction |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060902173022/http://jrbp.stanford.edu/db/projects/project_display.php?project_id=80 |archive-date=September 2, 2006 }}</ref>

The population-related disaster that Ehrlich predicted has failed to materialize, including the "hundreds of millions" of starvation deaths in the 1970s and the tens of millions of deaths in the United States in the 1970s and 1980s. Slowing of population growth rates and new food production technologies have increased the food supply faster than the population.<ref name="Haberman">{{cite web |last=Haberman |first=Clyde |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/06/01/us/the-unrealized-horrors-of-population-explosion.html |title=The Unrealized Horrors of Population Explosion |work=The New York Times |date=May 31, 2015 |access-date=March 13, 2023}}</ref> Ehrlich continued to stand by his general thesis that the human population is too large, posing a direct threat to human survival and the environment of the planet. In 2015, he stated that if he were to write the book then, "My language would be even more apocalyptic today."<ref name="Haberman"/> In 2018, he emphasized his view that the optimum population size is between 1.5 and 2 billion people.<ref name="Guardian2018"/> In 2022, he was a contributor to the "Scientists' warning on population", published by ''[[Science of the Total Environment]]'', which estimated that a [[sustainable population]] would be between 2 and 4 billion people.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crist|first1=Eileen|last2=Ripple|first2=William J.|author-link2=William J. Ripple|last3= Ehrlich|first3=Paul R.|author-link3=Paul R. Ehrlich|last4=Rees|first4=William E. |last5=Wolf |first5=Christopher |date=2022 |title=Scientists' warning on population |journal=[[Science of the Total Environment]] |volume=845 |article-number=157166 |url=https://scientistswarning.forestry.oregonstate.edu/sites/default/files/Crist2022.pdf |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2022.157166 |pmid= 35803428 |bibcode=2022ScTEn.84557166C |s2cid=250387801 |quote=Environmental analysts regard a sustainable human population as one enjoying a modest, equitable middle-class standard of living on a planet retaining its biodiversity and with climate-related adversities minimized. Analysts' estimate of that population size vary between 2 and 4 billion people, a figure obviously well below the present 7.9.}}</ref>

==<span class="anchor" id="Critics"></span>Reception==
===Responses to predictions===
During the 1960s and 70s when Ehrlich made his most alarming warnings, there was a widespread belief among experts that population growth presented an extremely serious threat to the future of human civilization, although differences existed regarding the severity of the situation, and how to decrease it.<ref name="dg" /><ref name="Leonhardt">{{Cite news | last=Leonhardt | first=David | title=Lessons From a Famous Bet | url=https://economix.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/09/30/lessons-from-a-famous-bet/ | access-date=October 24, 2013 | newspaper=The New York Times | date=September 30, 2013}}</ref>

In the decades since, critics have disputed Ehrlich's main thesis about overpopulation and its effects on the environment and human society, and his solutions, as well as his specific predictions made since the late 1960s.

[[File:Wheat yields in Least Developed Countries.svg|thumb|Wheat yields grew rapidly in [[Least Developed Countries]] since 1961.]]A common criticism is that Ehrlich's predictions routinely failed to come true; for instance, [[Ronald Bailey (writer)|Ronald Bailey]] of ''[[Reason (magazine)|Reason]]'' magazine has termed him an "irrepressible doomster&nbsp;... who, as far as I can tell, has never been right in any of his forecasts of imminent catastrophe."<ref name="Reason" /> On the first [[Earth Day]] in 1970, he warned that "[i]n ten years all important animal life in the sea will be extinct. Large areas of coastline will have to be evacuated because of the stench of dead fish."<ref name="Reason">{{Cite web | title=Cracked Crystal Ball: Environmental Catastrophe Edition | url=http://reason.com/blog/2010/12/30/cracked-crystal-ball-environme | work=reason.com – Free minds and free markets | publisher=Reason Foundation | access-date=March 4, 2013 | last=Bailey | first=Ronald | date=December 30, 2010}}</ref><ref name="foxnews">{{Cite news| title=Eight Botched Environmental Forecasts |url=https://www.foxnews.com/science/eight-botched-environmental-forecasts | date=December 30, 2010 | last=Lott | first=Maxim | work=FOX News | access-date=October 31, 2015 | quote=Again, not totally accurate, but I never claimed to predict the future with full accuracy}}</ref>

In a 1971 speech, he predicted that: "By the year 2000 the [[United Kingdom]] will be simply a small group of impoverished islands, inhabited by some 70 million hungry people." "If I were a gambler," Professor Ehrlich concluded before boarding an airplane, "I would take even money that [[England]] will not exist in the year 2000."<ref name="Reason" /><ref name="foxnews" />

When this scenario did not occur, he responded that "When you predict the future, you get things wrong. How wrong is another question. I would have lost if I had had taken the bet. However, if you look closely at England, what can I tell you? They're having all kinds of problems, just like everybody else."<ref name="Reason" />

Ehrlich wrote in ''The Population Bomb'' that, "India couldn't possibly feed two hundred million more people by 1980."<ref name="Population Bomb" /> In 1967, Ehrlich called to cut off emergency food aid to India as "hopeless".<ref name="Paying the Piper">{{cite journal |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Paul R. |title=Paying the Piper |journal=New Scientist |date=Dec 1967 |issue=14 |page=655}}</ref> This position was later criticized, as India's food production subsequently skyrocketed through the [[Green Revolution in India]], and its per capita caloric intake rose significantly in the following decades, even as its population doubled.<ref name="lomborg">{{Cite book |last1=Lomborg |first1=Bjørn |title=The skeptical environmentalist: Measuring the real state of the world |date=2002 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-0-521-01068-9 |pages=350–1 |title-link=The Skeptical Environmentalist}}</ref>

[[File:Felsoetold Wheat field, Hungary.jpg|thumb|250px|A large increase in global [[Agricultural productivity|food production]] since the 1960s and a slowing of [[population growth]] have, within the current context of continued depletion of [[non-renewable resource]]s, averted the scale of food shortage, [[famine]] and catastrophe foretold by the Ehrlichs.]]
Canadian journalist [[Dan Gardner (author)|Dan Gardner]], in his 2010 book ''Future Babble'',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2011/may/07/future-babble-dan-gardner-review |title=Future Babble by Dan Gardner – review |work=The Guardian |last=Evans |first=Dylan |date=May 7, 2011 |access-date=March 18, 2023 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201129193404/https://www.theguardian.com/books/2011/may/07/future-babble-dan-gardner-review |archive-date=November 29, 2020}}</ref> argues that Ehrlich has been insufficiently forthright in acknowledging errors he made, while being intellectually dishonest or evasive in taking credit for things he claims he got "right". For example, he rarely acknowledges the mistakes he made in predicting material shortages, massive death tolls from starvation (as many as one billion in the publication ''Age of Affluence'') or regarding the disastrous effects on specific countries. Meanwhile, he is happy to claim credit for "predicting" the increase of [[HIV/AIDS|AIDS]] or global warming.<ref name="dg" />

In the case of disease, Ehrlich had predicted the increase of a disease based on overcrowding, or the weakened immune systems of starving people, so it is "a stretch to see this as forecasting the emergence of AIDS in the 1980s." Similarly, global warming was one of the scenarios that Ehrlich described, so claiming credit for it, while disavowing responsibility for failed scenarios is a [[double standard]]. Gardner believes that Ehrlich is displaying classical signs of [[cognitive dissonance]], and that his failure to acknowledge obvious errors of his own judgement render his current thinking suspect.<ref name="dg" />

[[Barry Commoner]] has criticized Ehrlich's 1970 statement that "When you reach a point where you realize further efforts will be futile, you may as well look after yourself and your friends and enjoy what little time you have left. That point for me is 1972."<ref name="Commoner">{{Cite journal | journal=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists | first=Barry|last=Commoner | date=May 1972 | title=A Bulletin Dialogue: on "The Closing Circle"&nbsp;— Response | volume=28| issue=5| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pwsAAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA17 | pages=17–56| doi=10.1080/00963402.1972.11457931| url-access=subscription}}</ref> Gardner has criticized Ehrlich for endorsing the strategies proposed by William and Paul Paddock in their book ''[[Famine 1975! America's Decision: Who Will Survive?|Famine 1975!]]''. They had proposed a system of "triage" that would end food aid to "hopeless" countries such as India and Egypt. In ''Population Bomb'', Ehrlich suggests that "there is no rational choice except to adopt some form of the Paddocks' strategy as far as food distribution is concerned." Had this strategy been implemented for countries such as India and Egypt, which were reliant on food aid at that time, they would almost certainly have suffered famines.<ref name="dg" /> Instead, both Egypt and India have greatly increased their food production and now feed much larger populations without reliance on food aid.<ref name="lomborg" />{{unreliable source?|date=February 2023}}

===Left-wing critics===
Another group of critics, generally of the [[Left-wing politics|political left]], argues that Ehrlich emphasizes overpopulation too much as a problem in itself instead of distribution of resources.<ref name="The Population Bomb Revisited" /> [[Barry Commoner]] argued that Ehrlich emphasized overpopulation too much as the source of environmental problems, and that his proposed solutions were politically unacceptable because of the coercion that they implied, and because they would cost poor people disproportionately. He argued that technological, and above all social development would result in a natural decrease of both population growth and environmental damage.<ref>{{Cite journal | journal=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists | first=Barry|last=Commoner | date=May 1972 | title=A Bulletin Dialogue: on "The Closing Circle"&nbsp;— Response | volume=28| issue=5| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pwsAAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA17 | pages=17–56 | doi=10.1080/00963402.1972.11457931| quote=Population control (as distinct from voluntary, self-initiated control of fertility), no matter how disguised, involves some measure of political repression, and would burden the poor nations with the social cost of a situation&nbsp;— overpopulation&nbsp;— which is the current outcome of their previous exploitation, as colonies, by the wealthy nations.| url-access=subscription }}</ref> Ehrlich denies any type of racism, and has argued that if his policy ideas were implemented properly they would not be repressive.<ref>{{Cite book | title=The Race Bomb | year=1978 | publisher=Ballantine Books | last=Ehrlich | first=Paul | last2=Feldman | first2=Shirley }}</ref>

In a 2018 interview with ''The Guardian'', Ehrlich, while still proud of ''The Population Bomb'' for starting a worldwide debate on the issues of population, acknowledged weaknesses of the book including not placing enough emphasis on [[overconsumption]] and [[Economic inequality|inequality]], and countering accusations of racism. He argues "too many rich people in the world is a major threat to the human future, and cultural and genetic diversity are great human resources." He advocated for an "unprecedented redistribution of wealth" in order to mitigate the problem of overconsumption of resources by the world's wealthy, but said "the rich who now run the global system&nbsp;— that hold the annual 'world destroyer' meetings in Davos&nbsp;— are unlikely to let it happen."<ref name="Guardian2018">{{Cite news |last= Carrington|first=Damian|date=March 22, 2018 |title=Paul Ehrlich: 'Collapse of civilisation is a near certainty within decades'|url=https://www.theguardian.com/cities/2018/mar/22/collapse-civilisation-near-certain-decades-population-bomb-paul-ehrlich|work=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=April 4, 2018}}</ref>

Ehrlich and his colleague [[Rodolfo Dirzo]] argued in a 2022 perspective paper for the need to reduce fertility rates among "the overconsuming wealthy and middle classes", and wasteful consumption in general, with the ultimate goal being to reduce "the scale of the human enterprise" in order to mitigate the contemporary extinction crisis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dirzo|first1=Rodolfo|last2=Ceballos|first2=Gerardo|last3=Ehrlich|first3=Paul R.|author-link1=Rodolfo Dirzo|author-link3=Paul R. Ehrlich|date=2022 |title=Circling the drain: the extinction crisis and the future of humanity|journal=[[Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B]]|volume=377|issue=1857 |article-number=20210378 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2021.0378|pmid=35757873 |pmc=9237743 |s2cid=250055843 |quote=It is clear that only a giant change in human culture can significantly limit the extinction crisis. Humanity must face the need to reduce birth rates further, especially among the overconsuming wealthy and middle classes. In addition, a reduction of wasteful consumption will be necessary, accompanied by a transition away from environmentally malign technological choices such as private automobiles, plastic everything, and treating billionaires to space tourism. Otherwise growthmania will win; the human enterprise will not undergo the needed shrinkage, but will continue to expand, destroying most of biodiversity and further wrecking the life-support systems of humanity until global civilization collapses}}</ref>

===Simon–Ehrlich wager===
{{Main|Simon–Ehrlich wager}}

The economist [[Julian Simon]] argued in 1980 that overpopulation is not a problem as such and that humanity will adapt to changing conditions. Simon argued that eventually human creativity will improve living standards, and that most resources were replaceable.<ref>{{Cite journal | title=Resources, Population, Environment: An Oversupply of False Bad News | journal=Science | volume=208 | date=June 27, 1980 | pages=1431–1437 | issue=4451 | doi=10.1126/science.7384784 | pmid=7384784 | last1=Simon | first1=JL | jstor=1684670| bibcode=1980Sci...208.1431S }}</ref> Simon stated that over hundreds of years, the prices of virtually all commodities had decreased significantly and persistently.<ref>{{Cite book |title=The End of Doom |first=Ronald|last=Bailey |date=2015 |publisher=St. Martin's Press |isbn=978-1-250-05767-9 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/endofdoomenviron0000bail/page/38 38, 59] |quote=...nearly all resources in the past were much more expensive than they are today |author-link=Ronald Bailey (writer) |url=https://archive.org/details/endofdoomenviron0000bail/page/38 }}</ref> Ehrlich termed Simon the proponent of a "space-age cargo cult" of economists convinced that human creativity and ingenuity would create substitutes for scarce resources and reasserted the idea that population growth was outstripping the Earth's supplies of food, fresh water and minerals.<ref name="tierney1990" />

This exchange resulted in the [[Simon–Ehrlich wager]], a bet about the trend of prices for resources during a ten-year period that was made with Simon in 1980.<ref name="tierney1990">{{Cite news | last=Tierney | first= John | url= https://www.nytimes.com/1990/12/02/magazine/betting-on-the-planet.html?pagewanted=print&src=pm | title= Betting on the Planet | work=The New York Times | date= December 2, 1990 | access-date=September 26, 2012}}</ref> Ehrlich was allowed to choose ten commodities that he predicted would become scarce and thus increase in price. Ehrlich chose mostly metals, and lost the bet, as their average price decreased by about 30% in the next 10 years. Simon and Ehrlich could not agree about the terms of a second bet.{{citation needed|date=March 2026}}

===Ehrlich's response to critics===
Ehrlich argued that humanity has simply deferred the disaster by the use of more intensive agricultural techniques, such as those introduced during the [[Green Revolution]]. Ehrlich claimed that increasing populations and affluence are increasingly stressing the global environment, due to such factors as [[Biodiversity loss|loss of biodiversity]], [[overfishing]], [[global warming]], [[urbanization]], chemical pollution and competition for raw materials.<ref>{{Cite book | last=Ehrlich | first=Paul | last2=Ehrlich | first2=Anne | title=One with Nineveh: Politics, consumption, and the human future | publisher=Island Press | year=2004}}</ref> He maintained that due to growing global incomes, reducing consumption and human population is critical to protecting the environment and maintaining living standards, and that current rates of growth are still too great for a sustainable future.<ref>{{Cite news | title=Paul R. Ehrlich: Saving Earth | url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/la-xpm-2011-feb-12-la-oe-morrison-ehrlich-021211-story.html | access-date=March 4, 2013 | newspaper=Los Angeles Times | date=February 12, 2011 | last=Morrison | first=Patt | quote=Consumption is equally important. I'd think the biggest problem is figuring out what to do on consumption. We don't have any consumption condoms.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=Still Ticking | url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/29380/title/Still-Ticking/ | work=The Scientist | publisher=LabX Media Group | access-date=March 4, 2013 | first=Cristina|last=Luiggi | date=December 1, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last=Ehrlich | first=Paul R. | author2=Ehrlich, Anne H. | journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society | date=March 7, 2013 | volume=280 | issue=1754 | doi=10.1098/rspb.2012.2845 | pmid=23303549 | title=Can a collapse of global civilization be avoided? | article-number=20122845| pmc=3574335}} &nbsp; Also see: [http://rspb.royalsocietypublishing.org/content/280/1767/20131193#ref-1 Comment] by Prof. Michael Kelly, disagreeing with the paper by Ehrlich and Ehrlich; and [http://rspb.royalsocietypublishing.org/content/280/1767/20131373 response] by the authors.</ref><ref>{{Cite news | title=Green revolution could still blow up in our face | url=https://www.theage.com.au/national/green-revolution-could-still-blow-up-in-our-face-20080203-ge6oid.html | access-date=March 4, 2013 | newspaper=The Age | date=February 3, 2008 | first=Colin|last=Fraser | agency=Fairfax Media}}</ref>

==Other activities==
Ehrlich was one of the initiators of the group [[Population Connection|Zero Population Growth]], renamed Population Connection, in 1968, along with Richard Bowers and [[Charles Lee Remington]].{{Sfn |Dowbiggin |2008 |page=155}} In 1971, Ehrlich was elected to the [[Common Cause]] National Governing Board. He and his wife Anne were part of the board of advisers of the [[Federation for American Immigration Reform]] until 2003. He was a patron of [[Population Matters]], formerly known as the Optimum Population Trust.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Population Matters Patron | url=http://www.populationmatters.org/about/people/patrons/ | website=www.populationmatters.org | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140625195121/http://populationmatters.org/about/people/patrons/ | archive-date=June 25, 2014 }}</ref>

Consistent with his concern about the impact of pollution and in response to a doctoral dissertation by his student Edward Goth III, Ehrlich wrote in 1977 that, "Fluorides have been shown to concentrate in food chains, and evidence suggesting a potential for significant ecological effects is accumulating."<ref>Zelko F. Optimizing nature: Invoking the "natural" in the struggle over water fluoridation. History of Science. 2018; 1–22.</ref>

Ehrlich spoke at conferences in Israel on the issue of [[desertification]]. He argued "true Zionists should have small families".<ref name="haaretz">{{Cite news |url=https://www.haaretz.com/2012-12-06/ty-article/.premium/true-zionists-should-have-small-families/0000017f-ea2f-da9b-a1ff-ee6f58a00000 |title='True Zionists should have small families' suggests Paul Ehrlich, 40 years after writing 'The Population Bomb' |newspaper=[[Haaretz]] |first=Netta|last=Ahituv |date=December 6, 2012}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Ehrlich married Anne H. Ehrlich (née Howland) in December 1954. They had one daughter, Lisa Marie.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://icte.umsl.edu/WEArecipients/ehrlich.html | title=Whitney R. Harris World Ecology Center: Dr. Paul Ehrlich | publisher=icte.umsl.edu | access-date=June 21, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720092618/http://icte.umsl.edu/WEArecipients/ehrlich.html |archive-date=July 20, 2011 }}</ref> He announced that he had had a [[vasectomy]] in 1963 after his child's birth.{{Sfn |Dowbiggin |2008 |page=154, 168}}

===Death===
Ehrlich died of complications from cancer on March 13, 2026, at a retirement community where he lived in [[Palo Alto, California]]. He was 93.<ref name="schneider">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/15/books/paul-r-ehrlich-dead.html|title=Paul R. Ehrlich, Who Alarmed the World With 'The Population Bomb,' Dies at 93|publisher=The New York Times|date=March 15, 2026|accessdate=March 15, 2026|last=Schneider|first=Keith}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.miragenews.com/paul-r-ehrlich-population-bomb-author-dies-1637183/|title=Paul R Ehrlich, Population Bomb Author, Dies|publisher=Sustainable Population Australia|date=March 16, 2026|accessdate=March 16, 2026}}</ref>
